html:
A revolt by thousands of Igbo and Ibibio women in southeastern Nigeria in November and December 1929 against British colonial rule.

Britain ruled the region through indirect rule, using appointed warrant chiefs who were often corrupt and had no traditional standing. Men had been taxed since 1928. When a chief began counting women's property, the women believed they would be taxed next, at a time of falling palm oil prices.

The women used a traditional way of shaming men called "sitting on a man": they gathered at the chiefs' houses, sang, danced and refused to leave. The protest spread across the provinces of Owerri and Calabar. Women attacked Native Courts and European shops, including at the town of Aba. Troops opened fire, killing more than fifty women.

The colonial government gave up taxing women, abolished the warrant chief system and reformed local courts, and some women were appointed to them. The revolt is remembered as an early challenge to colonial rule in Nigeria and a landmark of women's protest.
sum: A revolt by thousands of Igbo and Ibibio women in southeastern Nigeria in November and December 1929 against British colonial rule.
